newsitem.title: USA: Family of sickened California girl sues juice firm.
newsitem.headline: Family of sickened California girl sues juice firm.

text.p: The family of a 2-year-old California girl who was hospitalized with kidney failure after allegedly drinking Odwalla apple juice has sued the company for damages, the family's attorney said Thursday.

In the lawsuit, filed in Superior Court in Alameda County, California, the family of Tara Azizi alleged that Odwalla Inc. engaged in the "negligent and careless preparation of an unpasteurized product so as to allow the presence of harmful, even toxic levels, of a strain of E. coli."
The suit also names Safeway Inc.. The family bought Odwalla juice at a Safeway store, the attorney said.
An Odwalla spokeswoman said the company would not comment on the suit.
Safeway spokeswoman Debra Lambert said she had yet to review the lawsuit but added that Safeway considered Odwalla "a full-service vendor."

"This product is delivered directly to our stores by Odwalla," Lambert said. "The product is rotated on the shelf by Odwalla, and it is contained for sale in a refrigerated unit that is in our produce department that is owned by Odwalla and maintained by Odwalla."

Tara Azizi became ill within days of consuming Odwalla apple juice in mid-October, her lawyer, Craig Needham, said. Toxicity from E. coli led to hospitalization, kidney failure and kidney dialysis, he said.
The girl was released from Children's Hospital Oakland on Tuesday and doctors said her prognosis for a full recovery was good. She had been hospitalized for about 20 days while undergoing treatment.
Dr. Rose Ellen Morrell, her doctor at the hospital, told reporters earlier this week that tests had not yet conclusively linked her illness to Odwalla apple juice.
About 50 people have fallen ill with E. coli bacterial infections in the Western United States and Canada in recent weeks, many after drinking Odwalla's unpasteurized apple juice.
Odwalla recalled 16 of its products immediately after the first E. coli cases were reported, removing them from store shelves in its distribution region.
Earlier this month, the outbreak claimed its first victim when a 15-month-old girl died in Denver.
A lawsuit was filed in Seattle against Odwalla and retailer Starbucks Corp. on behalf of a 6-year-old boy who required abdominal surgery after being infected.
